questions.question: An auditor asks who is responsible for hypervisor patching, physical-data-centre security, customer's EC2 guest OS hardening, and customer's IAM-policy design. The customer answers with one model published by AWS. Which is the correct division?
options: AWS manages every layer of the stack — hardware, hypervisor, network, guest OS, customer applications
Customers run physical datacentre security and operate the AWS global backbone network
AWS secures the cloud; customers secure what they put IN the cloud
AWS handles every compliance and regulatory requirement transparently for the customer
questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (hardware, facilities, global infrastructure). Customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (data, IAM, OS patching on EC2, etc.). The other options are incorrect: AWS manages every layer of the stack — hardware, hypervisor, network, guest OS, customer applications, IAM, and data — leaving customers no operational duties. Customers run physical datacentre security and operate the AWS global backbone network, while AWS only provisions virtual machines from the customer-built fleet. AWS handles every compliance and regulatory requirement transparently for the customer, with no shared duties on data, identity, or operating-system configuration.

questions.question: A team needs durable OBJECT storage for any size of file, REST-API-accessible, with 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability and globally addressable URLs. They don't need a POSIX filesystem. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EBS — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance
Amazon S3 — object storage with 11-nines durability, HTTPS REST access
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS filesystem shared across EC2 instances
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host
questions.explanation: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage service. It stores data as objects in buckets, offers 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EBS — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance; not globally addressable via URLs or designed for 11-nines durability. Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS filesystem shared across EC2 instances; not globally addressable via REST URLs with 11-nines object durability. EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host; data is lost on stop or termination and is not globally addressable.

questions.question: A startup wants the LOWEST latency for users in Tokyo, São Paulo, and Frankfurt. The architect proposes deploying the same application stack in AWS Regions geographically close to each user population (e.g., ap-northeast-1, sa-east-1, eu-central-1). What is the PRIMARY benefit of using these distinct Regions?
options: Lower latency to nearby users PLUS regional data-residency
Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region
Identical published prices across every Region
Free inter-Region data transfer for all active-active workloads
questions.explanation: Deploying into geographically closer Regions reduces latency for nearby users and supports data-residency requirements. AWS does NOT automatically replicate services across Regions; each service requires explicit configuration (S3 CRR, DynamoDB Global Tables, etc.). Per-Region pricing varies. Inter-Region traffic is billable. The other options are incorrect: Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region — false; cross-Region replication is optional, not the primary benefit of multi-Region deployments for user latency. Identical published prices across every Region — false; per-Region pricing varies and lower latency for local users is the primary benefit of geographic distribution. Free inter-Region data transfer for all active-active workloads — false; inter-Region transfer incurs data-transfer charges and is not a default benefit for users.

questions.question: A workload runs the SAME m5.large fleet 24×7 with no changes for the next 3 years. The finance team wants the BIGGEST possible compute discount in exchange for a multi-year commitment. Which EC2 pricing model fits?
options: On-Demand per-second pricing — pays the highest hourly rate and carries no commitment
Spot Instances — up to 90% off the On-Demand rate
Reserved Instances with a 3-year all-upfront term — up to 72% discount in exchange
Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation billing model used for licensing compliance
questions.explanation: For a STEADY, multi-year workload, the deepest discount comes from 3-year all-upfront Reserved Instances (up to 72%) or Compute Savings Plans (similar). On-Demand has NO commitment and NO discount. Spot is cheaper but interruptible. The other options are incorrect: On-Demand per-second pricing — pays the highest hourly rate and carries no commitment or discount in exchange for steady multi-year compute usage. Spot Instances — up to 90% off the On-Demand rate but interruptible; unsuitable for a steady multi-year workload that cannot tolerate reclaim events. Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation billing model used for licensing compliance; not the deepest-discount steady-multi-year-workload option for EC2 compute.

questions.question: A streaming site serves 90% static assets (videos, images) and is hit by viral traffic spikes from specific countries. Latency to those geographies dominates user-perceived performance. Which AWS service caches the assets at edge locations close to viewers and absorbs the spike load before it reaches the origin?
options: Amazon Route 53 — DNS routing service
AWS Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS for corporate traffic
Application Load Balancer — regional Layer-7 load balancer at the origin Region
Amazon CloudFront — global CDN with 600+ edge POPs caching static asset bytes
questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that distributes content from edge locations worldwide, reducing latency for end users by serving cached content from the nearest edge location. The other options are incorrect: Amazon Route 53 — DNS routing service; resolves names to endpoints but does not cache asset bytes at hundreds of edge POPs near viewers around the world. AWS Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS for corporate traffic; not a global CDN that caches static asset bytes near viewers. Application Load Balancer — regional Layer-7 load balancer at the origin Region; does not cache static asset bytes at hundreds of edge POPs near viewers.

questions.question: A developer needs to run a Python function in response to S3 object-creation events with NO server to provision, NO OS to patch, billing in 1 ms increments only when the function runs. Which AWS service fits?
options: AWS Lambda — serverless function-as-a-service: event-driven, no infra, per-ms billing
Amazon EC2 — a virtual-machine service that bills for provisioned capacity
Amazon ECS — a container-orchestration service that still requires provisioning a cluster
Amazon Lightsail — a bundled small-VM service with a flat monthly billing model
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. You upload code and Lambda runs it in response to events. You pay only for execution time — no server management required. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EC2 — a virtual-machine service that bills for provisioned capacity regardless of whether the function is executing; the customer manages the infra. Amazon ECS — a container-orchestration service that still requires provisioning a cluster; per-function event-driven billing is not part of its model. Amazon Lightsail — a bundled small-VM service with a flat monthly billing model; it is not an event-driven function-as-a-service.

questions.question: An EC2 instance must be granted read-only permission to a specific S3 bucket. Best practice in AWS is to attach a ROLE with the minimum permissions to the instance, not store an access key on disk. Which AWS service models who/what can do what on AWS resources via users, groups, roles, and policies?
options: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
AWS Internet Access Management
AWS Infrastructure and Application Management
AWS Image and AMI Management
questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you can do) in AWS through users, groups, roles, and policies. The other options are incorrect: AWS Internet Access Management — not a real AWS service; no service manages internet-access policies for instance roles, users, groups, or resources under that name. AWS Infrastructure and Application Management — not a real AWS service; AWS Systems Manager handles instance and application management but not the IAM users, groups, roles, and policies layer. AWS Image and AMI Management — not a real AWS service; AMI and image policies are managed through EC2 AMI controls, not a service that covers users, groups, instance roles, and resource policies.

questions.question: AWS infrastructure inside one Region is partitioned into multiple physically isolated facility groups, each with its OWN power, cooling, and network — connected to each other by sub-ms private fibre. A Region typically has 3+ of these. What's the AWS term for one of these facility groups?
options: Availability Zone — one or more discrete data-centre facilities with independent power
Region — the geographic area that contains and groups the AZs
Edge Location / CloudFront POP — a global edge-cache facility outside the Region structure
VPC subnet — a customer-defined logical network segment inside an AZ
questions.explanation: An AZ is one or more data centers within a Region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Multiple AZs in a Region enable high availability architecture. The other options are incorrect: Region — the geographic area that contains and groups the AZs; Regions share no power, cooling, or networking across their constituent AZs. Edge Location / CloudFront POP — a global edge-cache facility outside the Region structure; not an independently power- and cooling-isolated data-centre grouping. VPC subnet — a customer-defined logical network segment inside an AZ; not a physical power- and cooling-independent facility; subnets group connected IP address ranges sharing the AZ's underlying infrastructure.

questions.question: A regulated-industry customer running mission-critical workloads on AWS wants a named human on the AWS side: a Technical Account Manager who knows their architecture, reviews quarterly business reviews, and acts as their primary escalation. Which AWS Support plan includes a dedicated TAM by default?
options: Developer support — email-only support during business hours
Enterprise support — includes a dedicated Technical Account Manager who
Basic support — billing and account-help only
Business support — 24×7 phone/chat response and Trusted Advisor full checks
questions.explanation: The Enterprise Support plan includes a dedicated TAM, concierge support, and 15-minute response time for business-critical issues. Business plan has < 1 hour response. The other options are incorrect: Developer support — email-only support during business hours; it does not include a dedicated Technical Account Manager who knows the customer architecture. Basic support — billing and account-help only; it includes no technical support and no one who knows the customer architecture. Business support — 24×7 phone/chat response and Trusted Advisor full checks; it does not include a dedicated TAM who monitors critical workloads and provides architecture guidance ahead of incidents.

questions.question: The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars. ONE pillar covers the workload's ability to recover from failures, automatically scale, test recovery procedures, and meet RTO/RPO. Which pillar is this?
options: Security — protecting data + systems, but not the recover-from-failure pillar
Reliability — recovery from failure, scaling, testing recovery, RTO/RPO
Cost Optimisation — financial efficiency, not failure recovery
Performance Efficiency — using resources efficiently
questions.explanation: The Reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework focuses on recovery from disruptions, dynamic resource acquisition, and mitigating misconfigurations. The other options are incorrect: Security — protecting data + systems, but not the recover-from-failure pillar. Cost Optimisation — financial efficiency, not failure recovery. Performance Efficiency — using resources efficiently, not the same as reliability.

questions.question: A security audit asks: who made an `iam:DeleteUser` call against the production account at 14:47 UTC yesterday, from which IP, with which user-agent, and what parameters were used? The answer must come from the tenant-wide management-plane log. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch — aggregates metrics and application logs from AWS services and user-deployed agents
AWS CloudFormation — declarative IaC that provisions stacks from templates
AWS Transit Gateway — central networking hub for VPCs and on-prem connections
AWS CloudTrail — tenant-wide control-plane audit log: who called the API, when, from which IP
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records all API calls made to AWS services, providing an audit log of who did what, when, and from where. Essential for compliance and security investigations. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudWatch — aggregates metrics and application logs from AWS services and user-deployed agents; it does not record tenant-wide control-plane audit events showing who called which API, from which IP, at what time. AWS CloudFormation — declarative IaC that provisions stacks from templates; it does not record who invoked individual IAM user API calls or the source-IP parameters. AWS Transit Gateway — central networking hub for VPCs and on-prem connections; it does not log control-plane API calls, IAM identity, user-agent strings, or source IP the way CloudTrail does.

questions.question: An architect designs a NETWORK construct inside an AWS account that has customer-defined private IP ranges (CIDR), customer-defined subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, and security groups. The construct is LOGICALLY ISOLATED from other accounts. Which AWS resource is this?
options: An EC2 instance — a single virtual machine placed inside one of the customer-defined VPC subnets
The AWS global backbone — AWS private inter-Region fibre network
A Virtual Private Cloud — customer-defined logically isolated virtual network with CIDR, subnets per AZ
Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane that runs inside an existing logically isolated network
questions.explanation: A VPC is the canonical AWS virtual network primitive: customer-defined IP ranges, subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, SGs, gateways. The other options are incorrect: An EC2 instance — a single virtual machine placed inside one of the customer-defined VPC subnets; it is not itself the network construct that owns CIDR ranges, route tables, security groups, and NACLs. The AWS global backbone — AWS private inter-Region fibre network; it is not customer-controlled or logically isolated per account. Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane that runs inside an existing logically isolated network; it is not itself the network construct.

questions.question: Architecture-101 distinguishes two scaling models. Adding MORE machines and distributing load across them is one; replacing the existing machine with a BIGGER one is the other. Which mapping is correct?
options: Horizontal = use bigger instances
Horizontal scaling means adding database capacity only
The terms are interchangeable
Horizontal = scale OUT by adding instances; Vertical = scale UP to a larger instance
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out/in) adds/removes instances. Vertical scaling (scale up/down) resizes the instance to a larger/smaller type. AWS Auto Scaling handles horizontal scaling. The other options are incorrect: Horizontal = use bigger instances; Vertical = scale out by adding instances — reversed; horizontal means adding more instances while vertical means adding larger ones. Horizontal scaling means adding database capacity only; Vertical means adding compute instances — false; both terms apply across all resource types. The terms are interchangeable — false; adding more instances (horizontal) is distinct from adding larger capacity to a single instance (vertical).

questions.question: An architect needs to estimate the MONTHLY cost of a planned deployment (10 EC2 m6i.xlarge + 5 TB S3 Standard + 1 RDS db.m5.large + 100 GB data transfer) BEFORE provisioning anything. Which AWS tool produces a per-service estimate from the catalogue pricing?
options: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses already-incurred monthly cost data by service and tag
AWS Pricing Calculator — public web tool for estimating monthly cost from catalogue list
AWS Budgets — alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold on a live deployment
AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice recommendations on running infrastructure
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator lets you estimate monthly costs for AWS services before you deploy them. Cost Explorer analyzes existing costs; Budgets sets alerts. The other options are incorrect: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses already-incurred monthly cost data by service and tag; it is not a tool for estimating future transfer costs or pricing a proposed architecture before deployment. AWS Budgets — alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold on a live deployment; it is not a pre-deployment estimation tool and does not estimate the cost of anything before you deploy it. AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice recommendations on running infrastructure; it does not estimate pricing or model catalogue costs before any deployment.

questions.question: A web tier sized for steady traffic gets bursty afternoon spikes. The team wants the fleet to GROW to absorb peak and SHRINK when demand drops, automatically based on CPU and request-count metrics, without operator intervention. Which AWS feature?
options: EC2 instance-family swap — a manual right-sizing step performed on each instance
Automated OS patching via Systems Manager — applies security patches automatically but does not
AWS Auto Scaling — automatically adds or removes instances based on demand signals such as CPU
Scheduled RDS / EBS snapshots — automated backup operations that run on a time-based schedule
questions.explanation: AWS Auto Scaling monitors applications and automatically adjusts capacity (EC2 instances, ECS tasks, etc.) to maintain performance and minimize costs. The other options are incorrect: EC2 instance-family swap — a manual right-sizing step performed on each instance; it does not automatically add or remove capacity in response to traffic spikes. Automated OS patching via Systems Manager — applies security patches automatically but does not automatically scale capacity up or down based on load. Scheduled RDS / EBS snapshots — automated backup operations that run on a time-based schedule; they protect data but do not respond to request volume or automatically add compute capacity on demand.

questions.question: A finance team is comparing cloud to traditional data-centre TCO. The AWS sales rep keeps using the phrase 'pay only for what you use'. The finance lead asks for a concrete definition in pricing terms. Which best describes this principle?
options: Consumption-based pricing — billing is per actual usage with no upfront seat fee
Per-resource flat fee — a fixed pricing model that charges the same amount regardless of usage levels
Flat monthly subscription pricing — a fixed billing model that charges the same each month
Upfront annual licensing pricing — pays a fixed amount in advance for a year of access
questions.explanation: One of the key cloud benefits: consumption-based pricing. Unlike on-premises infrastructure with fixed costs, cloud billing is based on actual consumption. The other options are incorrect: Per-resource flat fee — a fixed pricing model that charges the same amount regardless of usage levels; not consumption-based pricing tied to actual usage. Flat monthly subscription pricing — a fixed billing model that charges the same each month regardless of actual resource consumption. Upfront annual licensing pricing — pays a fixed amount in advance for a year of access; not consumption-based pricing that scales with actual usage.

questions.question: A security investigator needs a per-API-call record: WHO (IAM principal), WHEN (timestamp), FROM WHERE (source IP / user-agent), WHAT (API name), WITH WHAT (request parameters). This is the AWS API auditing surface — distinct from metrics/logs aggregated by CloudWatch. Which AWS service provides exactly this audit trail?
options: AWS CloudTrail — records every API call across the account with caller
AWS Inspector — automated vulnerability assessment of EC2, Lambda, and ECR
AWS Config — resource-configuration history and rule evaluation
Amazon CloudWatch — metrics and application log aggregation
questions.explanation: CloudTrail is the AWS API-call audit log: every `Action` against any service is recorded with caller identity, time, source IP, user-agent, and parameters. CloudWatch is metrics + log aggregation — not the per-API audit trail. The other options are incorrect: AWS Inspector — automated vulnerability assessment of EC2, Lambda, and ECR; it does not record per-request API call history with IAM user, timestamp, or source-IP. AWS Config — resource-configuration history and rule evaluation; it does not record the IAM user agent, per-request timestamp, or source of individual API calls. Amazon CloudWatch — metrics and application log aggregation; it does not record the IAM user identity, request parameters, or source IP for each API call.

questions.question: A security team wants to grant the IAM principal `arn:aws:iam::111:role/web` access to a specific S3 bucket and deny everyone else. The control is written as a JSON document attached to the bucket itself (not to any IAM identity). Which control type is this?
options: An S3 bucket policy — a JSON resource policy attached to the bucket
An EC2 instance profile — attaches an IAM role so the instance can call AWS APIs
An S3 lifecycle policy — a JSON configuration that transitions or expires objects between storage classes
Default bucket encryption — a JSON configuration that encrypts new objects at rest
questions.explanation: S3 bucket policies are JSON-based resource policies that control who can access a bucket and what actions they can perform. They can grant access to other AWS accounts. The other options are incorrect: An EC2 instance profile — attaches an IAM role so the instance can call AWS APIs; it does not define allow or deny rules for which external principals may access the bucket itself. An S3 lifecycle policy — a JSON configuration that transitions or expires objects between storage classes; it does not control which principals can access bucket resources. Default bucket encryption — a JSON configuration that encrypts new objects at rest; it does not define which principals or ARNs are allowed or denied access to the bucket.

questions.question: A workload's web tier in a public subnet needs bidirectional internet connectivity. The route table for that subnet must have a default route pointing at a VPC-level component. Which component fits this role?
options: Internet Gateway — VPC-level horizontally scaled component that allows bidirectional
VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone with a route table entry
Network ACL — stateless subnet-level firewall evaluated on each packet
NAT Gateway — egress-only NAT for resources in private subnets to reach the internet
questions.explanation: An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally-scaled, redundant VPC component that enables communication between VPC instances and the internet. The other options are incorrect: VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone with a route table entry; it does not provide a default internet route or bidirectional internet connectivity. Network ACL — stateless subnet-level firewall evaluated on each packet; it filters traffic on a route but is not itself the component that provides internet connectivity. NAT Gateway — egress-only NAT for resources in private subnets to reach the internet; it does not enable inbound internet connectivity or serve as a default route for public subnets.

questions.question: A platform team manages 40 AWS resources across 3 environments. They want to declare the entire stack as code in JSON or YAML files, version-control it, do change-set previews before applying, and roll back on failure. Which AWS service is the native infrastructure-as-code engine?
options: Elastic Beanstalk — a PaaS that deploys application code and manages a stack of EC2, ELB, and Auto Scaling
OpsWorks — managed Chef and Puppet configuration management for an EC2 stack
AWS CloudFormation — declarative JSON/YAML templates over arbitrary AWS resources, with change sets
Systems Manager — fleet operations (patching, run-command, parameter store)
questions.explanation: AWS CloudFormation allows you to define AWS infrastructure as JSON or YAML templates and deploy it in a repeatable, automated way. The other options are incorrect: Elastic Beanstalk — a PaaS that deploys application code and manages a stack of EC2, ELB, and Auto Scaling; it does not manage arbitrary AWS resource stacks via declarative templates. OpsWorks — managed Chef and Puppet configuration management for an EC2 stack; it does not use JSON or YAML templates to declaratively define change sets across arbitrary AWS resource types. Systems Manager — fleet operations (patching, run-command, parameter store); it does not define or deploy a full declarative infrastructure stack from templates.

questions.question: A team needs to (a) register a `.com` domain, (b) host an authoritative DNS zone, (c) route users by geolocation/latency/weighted policies, (d) integrate health checks for failover. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon S3 + CloudFront — object storage and CDN for static content delivery
Amazon Route 53 — registers `.com` domains AND hosts authoritative DNS with routing policies
AWS Direct Connect + VPC peering — private network connectivity primitives
AWS Global Accelerator — anycast IP traffic acceleration that routes to healthy regional endpoints
questions.explanation: Route 53 is AWS's scalable DNS service. It routes users to applications, supports health checks, and offers routing policies like latency, geolocation, and failover. The other options are incorrect: Amazon S3 + CloudFront — object storage and CDN for static content delivery; neither provides domain registration, an authoritative DNS zone, nor route-policy-based traffic steering. AWS Direct Connect + VPC peering — private network connectivity primitives; neither registers domains, hosts DNS zones, nor provides routing policies like geolocation, weighted, or failover with health checks. AWS Global Accelerator — anycast IP traffic acceleration that routes to healthy regional endpoints; it does not register domains, host DNS zones, or provide geolocation, latency-based, or weighted routing policies.

questions.question: A team has medical imaging files that are accessed about 4× per year but, when accessed, must be retrievable in MILLISECONDS (not hours). They want to pay less than S3 Standard storage rates. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Standard-IA — same millisecond retrieval as Standard at a lower per-GB storage rate with a per-GB
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval times
S3 Standard — millisecond retrieval and lowest retrieval cost but the most expensive per-GB storage tier
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours-long retrieval and the cheapest storage
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA is for data accessed less frequently but needs immediate access when required. Lower storage cost than S3 Standard but retrieval fee applies. The other options are incorrect: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval times; cheaper storage but does not meet the millisecond-retrieval requirement for the medical imaging files. S3 Standard — millisecond retrieval and lowest retrieval cost but the most expensive per-GB storage tier; ill-suited for the infrequent-access pattern described. S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours-long retrieval and the cheapest storage; not a millisecond-retrieval tier for the medical imaging files described.

questions.question: A security architect drafts IAM policy for a new EC2 role. The role's job is to read ONE specific S3 bucket. Best practice says grant nothing beyond that exact need — not full S3, not even read on all buckets. Which IAM principle is this?
options: Least privilege — grant the MINIMUM permissions needed
Broad admin access — explicitly the opposite of least privilege
Shared IAM user across the team — anti-pattern
Long-lived access keys on users — anti-pattern
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task — nothing more. This minimizes the blast radius of compromised credentials. The other options are incorrect: Broad admin access — explicitly the opposite of least privilege; grant only the minimum permissions needed, not broad admin grants. Shared IAM user across the team — anti-pattern; sharing users removes the per-person audit trail and prevents granular least-privilege grant assignments. Long-lived access keys on users — anti-pattern; prefer short-lived role credentials over long-lived key grants that are harder to rotate.

questions.question: A web-server EC2 instance must accept HTTPS (TCP 443) from anywhere and SSH (TCP 22) only from the office IP. The control is a STATEFUL allow-only firewall attached to the instance's ENI, where outbound replies are auto-permitted by state. Which AWS control is this?
options: Network ACL — stateless, subnet-level, supports both allow and deny rules evaluated by rule number
EC2 Security Group — stateful, instance-level, allow-only rules with no explicit deny
IAM group — controls IAM administrator actions and policy attachment
VPC route table entry — controls how packets are routed between subnets and gateways
questions.explanation: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic automatically allowed) instance-level firewalls. You define allow rules only — there are no deny rules. Compare with Network ACLs which are stateless and subnet-level. The other options are incorrect: Network ACL — stateless, subnet-level, supports both allow and deny rules evaluated by rule number; not the stateful instance-attached allow-only control. IAM group — controls IAM administrator actions and policy attachment; not a firewall that filters HTTPS or SSH packets reaching an EC2 instance. VPC route table entry — controls how packets are routed between subnets and gateways; not a firewall that filters HTTPS or SSH packets per instance.

questions.question: An architect compares two VPC firewall constructs: (A) stateful, attached to ENIs, ALLOW-only, evaluates rules together; (B) stateless, attached to subnets, can ALLOW or DENY, evaluates rules in numbered order. Which mapping is correct?
options: Security Groups and NACLs are identical
Security Group = stateful, instance-level; NACL = stateless, subnet-level
NACLs are instance-level and Security Groups are subnet-level
SGs evaluate outbound only and NACLs evaluate inbound only
questions.explanation: SG: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), instance level, allow rules only, evaluated as a whole. NACL: stateless (return traffic needs explicit rule), subnet level, ordered allow/deny rules. instance-level, allow-only rules. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow AND deny rules. The other options are incorrect: Security Groups and NACLs are identical — false; SGs are stateful and allow-only while NACLs are stateless with numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order. NACLs are instance-level and Security Groups are subnet-level — reversed; NACLs apply at the subnet boundary with numbered rules while SGs apply at the instance ENI with stateful allow-only rules. SGs evaluate outbound only and NACLs evaluate inbound only — false; both Security Groups and NACLs evaluate both inbound and outbound traffic, with SGs being stateful and NACLs being stateless with explicit numbered deny rules.

questions.question: A relational database on EC2 needs PERSISTENT block storage that survives instance stop/start AND can be reattached to a different instance in the same AZ. The storage must be a /dev/sdX block device the OS formats with a filesystem. Which AWS storage primitive fits?
options: Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API
Amazon EBS — persistent block storage volume that outlives
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across instances
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host
questions.explanation: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage volumes attached to EC2. Unlike instance store, EBS persists after instance stop/terminate and can be detached/reattached. The other options are incorrect: Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API; not persistent block storage and not attachable to EC2 as a block device that survives instance stop. Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across instances; not a persistent single-instance block volume that presents as a raw block device. EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host; data is lost on stop or termination and cannot be detached and reattached to another instance the way EBS volumes can.

questions.question: A fleet of 12 EC2 web servers in 3 AZs must SHARE one writable filesystem so user uploads written by one server are immediately visible to the others. The filesystem must be POSIX with NFS-mount semantics, scale storage automatically, and be regional (multi-AZ). Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EFS — elastic NFS file system that mounts across many EC2 instances
Amazon EBS — single-instance persistent block storage
Amazon S3 — durable object storage
AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — a virtual tape library for backup workflows
questions.explanation: EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS file system that can be mounted to multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones simultaneously. Unlike EBS which attaches to one instance. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EBS — single-instance persistent block storage; multi-attach is limited to a few instances in the same AZ and is not designed as a writable shared filesystem across many instances in multiple AZs. Amazon S3 — durable object storage; accessible from any EC2 instance via REST API but not a POSIX writable filesystem mountable across a fleet. AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — a virtual tape library for backup workflows; not a writable shared filesystem for active production use across a fleet of web servers.

questions.question: EC2 instances in a PRIVATE subnet need OUTBOUND internet access (e.g., to call SaaS APIs and pull OS updates) WITHOUT being directly reachable from the internet inbound. Which VPC component provides outbound-only NAT for private subnets?
options: VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone
NAT Gateway — managed NAT service: private-subnet outbound to internet via Elastic IP
Internet Gateway — provides bidirectional internet connectivity for public subnet resources
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) — terminates IPsec VPN tunnels from on-prem into the VPC
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway = managed outbound-only NAT for private subnets, billed per hour + per GB. Internet Gateway = bidirectional. Virtual Private Gateway = IPsec VPN termination (a completely different service). The other options are incorrect: VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone; it provides no internet path and no outbound NAT for private subnet resources. Internet Gateway — provides bidirectional internet connectivity for public subnet resources; it is not an outbound-only inbound-blocked NAT for private subnet instances. Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) — terminates IPsec VPN tunnels from on-prem into the VPC; it provides no internet path for private subnet outbound traffic.

questions.question: A web tier has 6 EC2 instances serving HTTPS. A new release introduces autoscaling — at peak the fleet may grow to 30, at trough shrink to 3. The team needs a managed service that automatically registers/deregisters scaling instances and distributes inbound HTTPS requests with health checks. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudFront — a CDN that distributes cached content to edge locations
Amazon RDS read-replica — distributes read queries across database replicas
Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution of queries
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes inbound to EC2 / containers / IP
questions.explanation: ELB distributes traffic across multiple targets. ALB (Application) = Layer 7/HTTP, NLB (Network) = Layer 4/TCP, GLB (Gateway) = Layer 3 for third-party appliances. Integrates with Auto Scaling. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudFront — a CDN that distributes cached content to edge locations; it is not a back-end load balancer that distributes inbound HTTPS requests to EC2 instances with health checks. Amazon RDS read-replica — distributes read queries across database replicas; it is not a component that distributes inbound HTTPS traffic to web-tier EC2 instances. Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution of queries; it does not perform per-request inbound traffic distribution or health-check-based instance selection.

questions.question: A bucket holding critical compliance docs is at risk of accidental overwrite/delete by the application or by an admin. The team wants to retain a HISTORY of every object version, recover prior versions, and undelete tombstoned objects. Which S3 feature?
options: Bucket-creation order counter
Bucket-policy history — would track IAM-policy change versions if it existed
S3 Versioning — retains every version of every object; PUT and DELETE create new versions
S3 Object-level CloudTrail — audits API call events against objects including deletes but does not
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning stores all versions of an object including writes and deletes. Enables recovery from accidental overwrites/deletes. Can be used with Lifecycle policies to manage costs. The other options are incorrect: Bucket-creation order counter — not a real S3 feature; S3 does not keep an ordered creation counter or versions of bucket-creation events. Bucket-policy history — would track IAM-policy change versions if it existed; S3 does not natively retain versions of policy documents or deletion events. S3 Object-level CloudTrail — audits API call events against objects including deletes but does not retain previous version content or enable restoration of an earlier object version.

questions.question: An ops team wants automated recommendations across COST (idle resources, RI coverage), PERFORMANCE (under-provisioned instances), SECURITY (open SGs, root MFA), FAULT TOLERANCE (no Multi-AZ), and SERVICE LIMITS (approaching quotas) — refreshed continuously and surfaced in the console. Which AWS service?
options: External pen-test firm — a manual security engagement
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses resource-based policies for unintended external access
AWS Organizations — multi-account governance with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing
AWS Trusted Advisor — automated checks across five pillars with actionable recommendations
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides actionable recommendations. Basic checks (free): S3 bucket permissions, MFA on root account. Full checks require Business or Enterprise support. The other options are incorrect: External pen-test firm — a manual security engagement; it does not provide automated checks across cost optimisation, fault tolerance limits, or performance efficiency pillars. AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses resource-based policies for unintended external access; it does not emit cost, performance, or fault-tolerance recommendations across multiple service-pillar checks. AWS Organizations — multi-account governance with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing; it does not perform automated checks across the cost, fault tolerance, performance, and limits pillars.

questions.question: A new AWS account holder is reading the Free Tier offer. AWS publishes three categories: ALWAYS-FREE services, 12-MONTH free usage for new accounts, and SHORT-TRIAL free for specific services. Which describes the Free Tier correctly?
options: The Free Tier covers ALL services for the account lifetime with no limits
The Free Tier mixes 12-months-free offers for new accounts
The Free Tier covers only EC2 t-class instances for the first 30 days
The Free Tier is identical to a Reserved-Instance commitment with a specific short upfront payment
questions.explanation: AWS Free Tier includes: 12-month free (new accounts) — e.g., 750hr/month EC2 t2.micro; Always free — e.g., 1M Lambda requests/month; Trial — e.g., 2 months Amazon Redshift. The other options are incorrect: The Free Tier covers ALL services for the account lifetime with no limits — false; the Free Tier mixes 12-months-free offers for new accounts, always-free monthly allowances, and short-term trials. The Free Tier covers only EC2 t-class instances for the first 30 days — false; the Free Tier spans multiple services and mixes 12-months-free tiers, always-free allowances, and short-term trial offers. The Free Tier is identical to a Reserved-Instance commitment with a specific short upfront payment — false; Free Tier grants are always-free or time-limited with no payment commitment.

questions.question: A team needs a managed relational database with: (a) MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatibility (zero application change), (b) auto-scaling storage up to 128 TB, (c) up to 15 low-latency cross-AZ read replicas, (d) standard AWS billing per second. Which managed RDS engine fits ALL four?
options: DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value store
ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value cache with auto-scaling cluster nodes
Amazon Aurora — managed RDBMS with auto-scaling storage to 128 TB
Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse with auto-scaling storage
questions.explanation: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational database. It auto-scales storage, replicates across 3 AZs with 6 copies, and offers serverless options. Fully managed within RDS. The other options are incorrect: DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value store; it is not MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible and does not provide low-latency read replicas in a relational engine the way Aurora does. ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value cache with auto-scaling cluster nodes; fast but not a durable relational database with auto-scaling storage and SQL latency guarantees. Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse with auto-scaling storage; not MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible and not designed for OLTP latency workloads.

questions.question: A Lambda function must read from DynamoDB and write to S3. The team wants AWS BEST PRACTICE for credentials: NO long-lived access keys baked into the function code or env vars; AWS auto-injects temporary credentials when the function runs. Which IAM construct does this?
options: IAM User with access keys — long-lived credentials that must be manually rotated
IAM Role assumed via STS — short-lived temporary credentials auto-vended
IAM Group — a collection of users that inherits policies
IAM Policy document — describes permissions but is not itself a principal
questions.explanation: IAM Roles are assumable identities with permissions. EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and cross-account users assume roles. No static credentials — uses temporary security tokens via STS. The other options are incorrect: IAM User with access keys — long-lived credentials that must be manually rotated; an anti-pattern for Lambda or any compute identity because temporary auto-vended credentials are not used. IAM Group — a collection of users that inherits policies; cannot itself execute Lambda functions or receive temporary auto-vended credentials from STS. IAM Policy document — describes permissions but is not itself a principal; it cannot assume roles, execute Lambda, or hold auto-refreshing temporary credentials.

questions.question: A web tier writes 'order placed' events to a backend that must NOT lose messages even if the consumer is down for hours. The consumer is a worker fleet that PULLS messages, processes them, and explicitly deletes them. Which AWS service fits this decoupling pattern?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — ordered event stream for real-time consumer processing
AWS Step Functions — state-machine orchestration for coordinating consumer workflows
Amazon SNS — push-based pub/sub fan-out that delivers messages to topic subscribers
Amazon SQS — managed pull-based message queue with visibility timeout
questions.explanation: SQS (Simple Queue Service) decouples microservices by providing a durable message buffer. Producers send messages; consumers poll and process them. Prevents data loss if a consumer fails. The other options are incorrect: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — ordered event stream for real-time consumer processing; messages are retained for hours/days but it is not the canonical durable pull-queue for fire-and-forget consumer decoupling. AWS Step Functions — state-machine orchestration for coordinating consumer workflows; it does not queue or retain messages independently of the workflow state. Amazon SNS — push-based pub/sub fan-out that delivers messages to topic subscribers; it is not a durable pull-based consumer queue with visibility timeout and dead-letter support.

questions.question: An architect compares two AWS messaging services: (A) pull-based; consumer reads, processes, and deletes; one-to-one with the worker fleet. (B) push-based pub/sub; topic broadcasts to many subscribers (Lambda, SQS, email, SMS, HTTPS). Which is which?
options: They are functionally identical
SNS retains messages durably and SQS does not
SQS = pull-based queue for decoupling; SNS = push-based pub/sub for fan-out
SQS is for email push delivery and SNS is for application pull queuing
questions.explanation: SQS: one consumer polls messages from a queue (point-to-point). SNS (Simple Notification Service): one message fan-out to multiple subscribers (email, SQS, Lambda, HTTP) simultaneously. The other options are incorrect: They are functionally identical — false; SQS is pull-based durable queue storage while SNS is push-based pub/sub fan-out to multiple subscriber endpoints. SNS retains messages durably and SQS does not — false; SQS is the durable pull-based message store with configurable retention, while SNS push-delivers and does not retain messages. SQS is for email push delivery and SNS is for application pull queuing — reversed and incorrect; SQS is the pull-based queue and SNS provides the push-based fan-out.

questions.question: A 300 TB media archive sits in an on-prem data centre with a 1 Gbps internet uplink. Online transfer would take weeks. AWS offers a physical appliance shipped to the customer site for offline bulk transfer (encrypted at rest, returned for ingest). Which service?
options: AWS Disaster Recovery / Elastic DR — orchestrates online replication and failover
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — a cold storage class for long-term retention
Amazon CloudFront — a global CDN that caches and delivers content online
AWS Snowball / Snowball Edge — rugged physical appliance for offline bulk dataset
questions.explanation: AWS Snowball is a secure, physical appliance for offline data migration. 80TB capacity. Snowball Edge adds compute. Snowmobile is a 100PB truck for exabyte migrations. The other options are incorrect: AWS Disaster Recovery / Elastic DR — orchestrates online replication and failover; it is not a physical bulk-data offline transfer service for moving 300 TB off slow internet links. S3 Glacier Deep Archive — a cold storage class for long-term retention; it is not an offline bulk-transfer appliance for initial data migration when online transfer is too slow. Amazon CloudFront — a global CDN that caches and delivers content online; it is not an offline bulk data-transfer service for large-scale migration from on-premises.

questions.question: A small dev team wants to deploy a Node.js web app to AWS without configuring the underlying EC2 / LB / autoscaling / health-checks themselves. They upload the source, AWS provisions everything based on the platform, scales it, and updates it. Which AWS service fits?
options: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane
Amazon ECR — managed container image registry
AWS CDK — Infrastructure-as-Code tool that synthesises CloudFormation
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS that provisions EC2, load balancer
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS that deploys web apps (Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Docker). You upload code; Beanstalk handles the infrastructure. You still control the underlying resources. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane; the team still configures autoscaling policies, health checks, and deploy pipelines manually rather than getting them provisioned automatically. Amazon ECR — managed container image registry; it stores and versions container images but does not provision load balancers, Auto Scaling, or platform updates. AWS CDK — Infrastructure-as-Code tool that synthesises CloudFormation; the team still provisions and manages the underlying infrastructure and platform updates.

questions.question: All web traffic must be encrypted in transit. The certificate that proves the server's identity and enables TLS handshakes must be (a) trusted by every modern browser, (b) issued / renewed automatically by AWS at no cost, (c) usable on ALB + CloudFront + API GW. Which AWS service issues these public TLS certs?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice checks
AWS Certificate Manager — issues and auto-renews free public TLS certificates for use
AWS Secrets Manager — stores and rotates application secrets such as database passwords
AWS KMS — manages encryption keys for data-at-rest operations
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS/SSL for encryption. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions and manages free public SSL/TLS certificates for use with ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway. The other options are incorrect: AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice checks; it does not issue TLS certificates and issues no authority over domain identity verification or certificate lifecycle management. AWS Secrets Manager — stores and rotates application secrets such as database passwords; it does not issue public TLS certificates for use on CloudFront distributions or ALB listeners. AWS KMS — manages encryption keys for data-at-rest operations; it does not issue TLS certificates or manage certificate renewal for HTTPS endpoints.

questions.question: An analytics team runs SQL queries over 500 TB of clickstream data. The workload is read-heavy, scans large columns of a few facts at a time, joins to dimension tables, and benefits from columnar compression + MPP (massively parallel processing). Which AWS service?
options: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value cache for sub-millisecond data reads
RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL — managed OLTP relational database optimised for transactional data
Amazon Redshift — managed columnar data warehouse with massively parallel processing
DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value and document store for fast single-key data access
questions.explanation: Redshift is AWS's managed data warehouse for analytics (OLAP). Uses columnar storage and MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) to run complex analytical queries across petabytes of data. The other options are incorrect: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value cache for sub-millisecond data reads; not a massively parallel SQL engine designed for scanning columnar analytics facts at petabyte scale. RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL — managed OLTP relational database optimised for transactional data; not a massively parallel columnar processing engine for petabyte analytics. DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value and document store for fast single-key data access; not a massively parallel SQL data warehouse for complex analytics over petabytes.

questions.question: A compliance team needs the AWS service that: (a) takes a snapshot of every resource's CONFIGURATION over time, (b) evaluates each snapshot against rules (e.g., 'S3 bucket must have versioning enabled'), (c) surfaces drift with timeline + non-compliant flag. Which service?
options: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 instances via patching, session manager, and run command
AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates against rules
AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 or Lambda targets
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants for unintended external access
questions.explanation: AWS Config is the configuration-recording / rule-evaluation service. CodeDeploy deploys application code. Systems Manager is run-time admin. The other options are incorrect: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 instances via patching, session manager, and run command; it does not record resource configuration history or evaluates account-wide compliance rules against snapshots. AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 or Lambda targets; it does not track resource configuration history or evaluate AWS resources against compliance rules. AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants for unintended external access; it does not record general resource configuration history or evaluate resources against custom compliance rules.

questions.question: A public-facing web tier is hit with a sustained Layer-3/4 volumetric DDoS (SYN floods, UDP reflection). The customer wants automatic, no-config-required L3/L4 DDoS protection AT NO ADDITIONAL CHARGE; for the higher tier (cost-protection guarantees, DDoS Response Team access) they're willing to pay extra. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Shield — L3/L4 DDoS protection at the AWS edge, automatic for all customers with no configuration required
AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules engine on top of ALB or API Gateway
AWS KMS — managed encryption-key service for encrypt/decrypt
AWS Certificate Manager — issues and renews TLS certificates for AWS integrations
questions.explanation: AWS Shield Standard: free, automatic DDoS protection for all AWS customers. Shield Advanced: paid, enhanced protection for EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53 with the DDoS Response Team (DRT) and financial protection. The other options are incorrect: AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules engine on top of ALB or API Gateway; it is not an automatic DDoS protection layer; separate WAF rules are required to handle L7 attacks. AWS KMS — managed encryption-key service for encrypt/decrypt; DDoS protection is not its function and no automatic L3/L4 protection is provided or required from KMS. AWS Certificate Manager — issues and renews TLS certificates for AWS integrations; it provides no DDoS protection and no automatic L3/L4 mitigation is required from ACM.

questions.question: A telemetry pipeline must ingest 1 million events/sec from IoT devices, retain them ordered for 24-168 hours, and let multiple consumers replay the stream (Lambda, Firehose to S3, Analytics with windowing). Which AWS service is the streaming primitive?
options: Amazon RDS — managed relational database for persistent transactional data
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — managed, shard-partitioned
Amazon S3 — durable object store that can act as a Kinesis Firehose destination
Amazon SQS — pull-based message queue with visibility timeout
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is the streaming primitive: shard-partitioned, ordered within a shard, retention 24-168 hours, multiple consumers can replay. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS — managed relational database for persistent transactional data; it is not a real-time stream ingestion primitive for 1 million events per second. Amazon S3 — durable object store that can act as a Kinesis Firehose destination; it is not a real-time stream ingestion service capable of one-million-events-per-second ingest. Amazon SQS — pull-based message queue with visibility timeout; messages are consumed once and deleted by a single consumer group with no ordered replay capability for multiple independent consumers.

questions.question: An e-commerce ALB-fronted app is being probed with SQLi and XSS payloads. The team wants Layer-7 HTTP request inspection that blocks known bad patterns (OWASP Top 10 managed rule groups) and rate-limits abusive sources — without code change. Which AWS service?
options: Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnels between on-prem and AWS
VPC Flow Logs with ML detection — captures flow-record metadata for traffic anomaly analysis
AWS Network Firewall — Layer-3/4 stateful firewall at the VPC boundary
AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP inspection engine with managed rule groups for SQLi, XSS, bad actors
questions.explanation: AWS WAF filters web traffic to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AppSync. You create rules to allow/block requests based on IP, headers, body content, or SQL/XSS patterns. The other options are incorrect: Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnels between on-prem and AWS; it does not provide Layer-7 HTTP rule groups for blocking SQLi, XSS, or IP-rate-limiting on an ALB. VPC Flow Logs with ML detection — captures flow-record metadata for traffic anomaly analysis; it does not perform deep packet inspection of HTTP payloads for SQLi or XSS rule matching. AWS Network Firewall — Layer-3/4 stateful firewall at the VPC boundary; it does not inspect HTTP payloads for SQLi or XSS and does not apply managed rule groups at the ALB request rate.

questions.question: A read-heavy product-detail page has 70% of requests hitting the database for the SAME 10 000 hot keys. The team wants to put a sub-millisecond key-value cache IN FRONT of the database with TTL-based invalidation. Which AWS service?
options: RDS read replicas — asynchronously replicate the primary RDS database to scale relational read traffic
Amazon ElastiCache — managed in-memory cache offering sub-millisecond reads in front of the database
Amazon CloudFront — content-delivery network that caches HTTP responses at edge POPs
DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) — DynamoDB-specific in-memory accelerator
questions.explanation: ElastiCache reduces database load by caching frequent queries in memory. Redis supports persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets. Memcached is simpler, multi-threaded. Both offer microsecond read latency. The other options are incorrect: RDS read replicas — asynchronously replicate the primary RDS database to scale relational read traffic; not a sub-millisecond in-memory key-value front for the database. Amazon CloudFront — content-delivery network that caches HTTP responses at edge POPs; not a sub-millisecond in-memory key-value front for the database. DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) — DynamoDB-specific in-memory accelerator; useful for DynamoDB but not a generic sub-millisecond cache in front of an arbitrary database.

questions.question: A container team wants to run Docker workloads on AWS without managing any EC2 worker nodes — AWS picks the underlying compute, scales it, patches it. The team only declares CPU / memory per task. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EKS with managed node groups — managed Kubernetes control plane
ECS on the EC2 launch type — Amazon manages the control plane but the customer manages the underlying
AWS Fargate — serverless container runtime; AWS owns the underlying compute
AWS Lambda — function-as-a-service for event-driven code execution
questions.explanation: AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers (used with ECS or EKS). No EC2 instances to manage — you define CPU/memory requirements, and AWS handles the infrastructure. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EKS with managed node groups — managed Kubernetes control plane; the underlying EC2 compute nodes are still the customer's responsibility to patch and manage. ECS on the EC2 launch type — Amazon manages the control plane but the customer manages the underlying EC2 worker compute fleet. AWS Lambda — function-as-a-service for event-driven code execution; the underlying compute is serverless but Lambda is not designed for running arbitrary long-lived container workloads.

questions.question: A multi-region application wants ANYCAST IP entry points: users globally connect to a single static IP that the AWS network routes over its backbone to the closest healthy regional endpoint, with sub-second failover on regional health degradation. Which service?
options: Amazon CloudFront — CDN that accelerates HTTP content delivery via the AWS backbone to edge caches
Amazon Route 53 — DNS service with routing policies including latency-based routing to the closest
AWS Global Accelerator — two static anycast IPs that route over the AWS backbone to the closest healthy
Application Load Balancer — a regional Layer-7 load balancer that routes to healthy targets within one
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator uses AWS's private global network (not the internet) to route traffic to the optimal regional endpoint, reducing latency and improving failover for global applications. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudFront — CDN that accelerates HTTP content delivery via the AWS backbone to edge caches; it does not provide anycast static IPs for non-HTTP TCP/UDP application traffic. Amazon Route 53 — DNS service with routing policies including latency-based routing to the closest healthy endpoint; it relies on resolver caching and does not provide anycast IPs. Application Load Balancer — a regional Layer-7 load balancer that routes to healthy targets within one Region; it does not route globally to the closest healthy endpoint across Regions.

questions.question: An RDS engineer compares two HA-vs-scaling options: (A) a synchronous standby in a different AZ that the engine auto-fails-over to on primary failure; (B) asynchronous COPY replicas in the same or other Region that take read traffic to scale OUT reads. Which mapping is correct?
options: Multi-AZ and Read Replicas are functionally interchangeable
Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup
Multi-AZ = synchronous standby for HA; Read Replicas = asynchronous read scaling
Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in different AZ for failover HA — automatic failover ~1-2min. Read Replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling — promotes manually for DR. Both can exist simultaneously. The other options are incorrect: Multi-AZ and Read Replicas are functionally interchangeable — false; Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby failover for high availability while Read Replicas provide asynchronous scaling for read throughput. Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup — false; automated backups handle that; Read Replicas use asynchronous replication for scaling read queries, not for synchronous failover standby. Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR — false; Multi-AZ is an in-Region synchronous standby HA mechanism; cross-Region DR uses asynchronous Read Replicas in other Regions.

questions.question: An auditor asks for the customer's most recent SOC 2 Type 2, PCI-DSS AOC, and ISO 27001 certificate from AWS. The customer needs a self-service portal that issues download-on-demand attestations. Which AWS service?
options: AWS CodeCommit — managed Git source-code repository
Amazon ECR — managed container image registry for Docker images
AWS Artifact — self-service portal that issues
AWS CodeBuild — managed CI build service
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS's compliance documentation: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, HIPAA reports, and agreements. Useful for enterprise compliance and audits. The other options are incorrect: AWS CodeCommit — managed Git source-code repository; it does not provide a self-service portal that issues or offers download-on-demand compliance reports. Amazon ECR — managed container image registry for Docker images; it does not host or issue downloadable compliance certifications or audit reports. AWS CodeBuild — managed CI build service; it does not provide a self-service portal for issuing or downloading AWS compliance reports on demand.

questions.question: A compliance team wants S3 buckets continuously scanned to find objects containing PII / PHI / credentials. The scanner must classify with ML, emit findings into Security Hub, and not require shipping bucket contents externally. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon GuardDuty — analyses VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail API events for threat detection
AWS Network Firewall — Layer-3/4 stateful firewall for VPC-level traffic
Amazon Macie — managed ML-based sensitive-data discovery on S3 (PII, credentials, etc.)
AWS KMS — manages encryption keys for AWS services
questions.explanation: Macie uses machine learning to automatically discover and protect sensitive data (PII, financial data) in S3 buckets, identifying overly permissive access or sensitive data exposure. The other options are incorrect: Amazon GuardDuty — analyses VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail API events for threat detection; it does not scan S3 object content for PII or exposed credentials. AWS Network Firewall — Layer-3/4 stateful firewall for VPC-level traffic; it does not scan S3 object content for sensitive data or credentials. AWS KMS — manages encryption keys for AWS services; it does not scan S3 bucket contents for PII or credentials.

questions.question: A SOC wants AUTOMATED, MACHINE-LEARNING-BASED threat detection on AWS API activity (CloudTrail), VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 DNS. The service must flag known IoCs, anomalous behaviour, and cryptocurrency-mining EC2s — with NO agent on instances. Which AWS service?
options: AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules engine in front of ALB and CloudFront
Endpoint AV on each EC2 — agent-based protection for known malware on individual instances
Inline VPC IDS appliance — a third-party network intrusion-detection device
Amazon GuardDuty — agentless machine-learning detection across CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs
questions.explanation: GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to detect unusual API calls, unauthorized deployments, cryptocurrency mining, and compromised instances — with no agents to install. The other options are incorrect: AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules engine in front of ALB and CloudFront; it does not perform machine-learning threat detection on CloudTrail logs, VPC flow logs, or Route 53 DNS IOCs. Endpoint AV on each EC2 — agent-based protection for known malware on individual instances; it does not perform machine-learning analysis of CloudTrail events or account-wide API activity. Inline VPC IDS appliance — a third-party network intrusion-detection device; it does not perform cloud-native machine-learning analysis of CloudTrail API activity or known-IOC correlation.

questions.question: A FinOps analyst wants to (a) chart historical spend per service / per tag / per linked account, (b) compare last quarter to this, (c) drill into cost spikes. The analysis is over ALREADY-INCURRED costs, not estimates. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Pricing Calculator — a free pre-deployment estimation tool for a proposed architecture
AWS Budgets — sets cost and usage thresholds for an account and sends alerts on spikes
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises and analyses actual AWS cost
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for compliance reports
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer lets you analyze historical cost trends, identify cost drivers, forecast future spend, and find optimization opportunities with detailed filtering and charting. The other options are incorrect: AWS Pricing Calculator — a free pre-deployment estimation tool for a proposed architecture; it does not let you drill into historical service spend or compare actual versus forecast cost by period. AWS Budgets — sets cost and usage thresholds for an account and sends alerts on spikes; it does not chart historical service-level spend or provide the analytical views Cost Explorer offers. AWS Artifact — self-service portal for compliance reports; it has no cost visualisation, historical account spend analysis, or cost-spike detection capability.

questions.question: A company has 40+ AWS accounts. They want one place to: (a) create new accounts, (b) cluster them into OUs, (c) apply guardrails via Service Control Policies, (d) consolidate billing into one invoice. Which AWS service?
options: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO and permission-set assignment across multiple AWS accounts
AWS Migration Hub — tracks application migrations across AWS tools
AWS Organizations — central multi-account management plane with OUs, Service Control Policies
AWS Auto Scaling — coordinates dynamic capacity scaling across multiple AWS services
questions.explanation: AWS Organizations enables centralized management of multiple AWS accounts: consolidated billing (volume discounts), Service Control Policies to restrict account permissions, and account grouping in OUs. The other options are incorrect: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO and permission-set assignment across multiple AWS accounts; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and billing. AWS Migration Hub — tracks application migrations across AWS tools; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, Service Control Policies, and consolidated billing. AWS Auto Scaling — coordinates dynamic capacity scaling across multiple AWS services; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing.

questions.question: Inside AWS Organizations, a permission GUARDRAIL applies at the OU or account level. It can DENY (or filter) what any IAM principal — including the account's root user — is allowed to do. It does NOT grant permissions, only caps them. Which construct is this?
options: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users, groups, or roles
A Service Control Policy (SCP) at the OU or account scope — the GUARDRAIL that caps maximum permissions
A VPC-level network ACL filtering subnet traffic — an account-level networking control
A CloudFormation template that provisions account resources — IaC for deploying infrastructure
questions.explanation: SCPs are the AWS Organizations guardrail: they cap (deny / filter) the maximum permissions for IAM principals in the targeted OU / account, including the account's root user. They never GRANT — they only restrict. The other options are incorrect: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users, groups, or roles — grants permissions within a single account; it does not cap the maximum permissions across an OU or multiple accounts like an SCP. A VPC-level network ACL filtering subnet traffic — an account-level networking control; it does not cap IAM permissions or enforce account-level permission guardrails. A CloudFormation template that provisions account resources — IaC for deploying infrastructure; it does not enforce permission caps or serve as a permission guardrail across accounts.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor wants to publish their product as an AMI that AWS customers can deploy, with metered billing on hourly or per-API-call basis, with consolidated invoicing through the customer's AWS bill. Which AWS feature publishes/buys SaaS, AMIs, and containers?
options: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party AMIs, SaaS, containers
AWS Marketplace for branded hardware
AWS Careers portal — for recruiting job openings
AWS RI Marketplace — secondary market for selling unused Reserved Instance commitments
questions.explanation: AWS Marketplace lets customers find, subscribe to, and deploy third-party software that runs on AWS. Includes security, networking, data, ML, and business intelligence tools with flexible billing. The other options are incorrect: AWS Marketplace for branded hardware — not a real AWS product; AWS Marketplace sells third-party software AMIs, SaaS subscriptions, containers, and data products — not physical hardware. AWS Careers portal — for recruiting job openings; it is not a catalogue for selling AMIs, SaaS, containers, or hourly-billed third-party software products. AWS RI Marketplace — secondary market for selling unused Reserved Instance commitments; it does not host third-party AMIs, SaaS subscriptions, or hourly call-based metered billing products.

questions.question: A cloud-101 lecture defines a property as: 'resources can be ADDED or REMOVED automatically in response to demand signals, and you pay only for actual usage'. This contrasts with the on-prem paradigm of static, over-provisioned peak capacity. Which cloud property is this?
options: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware bought ahead of demand
Automatic scaling up AND down with demand, paying for actual usage — the textbook elasticity property
Annual long-horizon capacity planning with a fixed reserved allocation — a traditional procurement model
Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load even when actual demand is low — the opposite
questions.explanation: Elasticity = dynamically scale resources with demand + pay for actual usage. The other options are incorrect: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware bought ahead of demand — not a cloud property; this is the traditional fixed-allocation model that does not scale with actual usage. Annual long-horizon capacity planning with a fixed reserved allocation — a traditional procurement model; it does not automatically scale with actual usage or represent a cloud elasticity property. Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load even when actual demand is low — the opposite of the cloud elasticity property; resources are provisioned regardless of actual usage.

questions.question: An app-sec team wants ongoing CVE scanning of running EC2 instances (kernel + installed packages) AND of Lambda function dependencies, with findings emitted into Security Hub. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend across accounts and services
AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates compliance rules
AWS Artifact — provides downloadable compliance reports and agreements
Amazon Inspector — automated vulnerability assessment of EC2 / Lambda / ECR
questions.explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically scans for known CVEs in running EC2/Lambda workloads and checks for unintended network accessibility (e.g., open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0), providing prioritized findings. The other options are incorrect: AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend across accounts and services; it does not scan Lambda functions for CVEs or emit security findings to the Security Hub findings schema. AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates compliance rules; it does not scan packages for CVEs or produce vulnerability findings emitted to the Security Hub findings schema. AWS Artifact — provides downloadable compliance reports and agreements; it does not scan for security vulnerabilities or emit CVE findings from running EC2 instances.

questions.question: An auditor asks AWS who is responsible for: (1) the physical security of the data centre, (2) hypervisor patching, (3) the customer's EC2 guest OS patching, (4) the customer's application data encryption. Which mapping is correct under the Shared Responsibility Model?
options: Customer owns ALL four items
AWS owns ALL four items
Mapping varies by support tier
AWS = security OF the cloud; Customer = security IN the cloud
questions.explanation: AWS: physical security, data center facilities, networking hardware, hypervisor, and managed service infrastructure. Customer: everything they put in the cloud — data encryption, IAM, OS patching on EC2, network config. The other options are incorrect: Customer owns ALL four items — incorrect; AWS owns the security of the cloud foundation including datacentre, hardware, hypervisor, and network. AWS owns ALL four items — incorrect; customers own security IN the cloud, including guest OS patching, IAM, data, and application configuration. Mapping varies by support tier — incorrect; the shared-responsibility model is fixed and not influenced by which support tier the account holds.

questions.question: A platform team wants ONE place to collect logs from: EC2 (via agent), Lambda (auto-stream), ECS containers, on-prem servers (agent), VPC Flow Logs. The destination must let them query with a SQL-like language, set retention, and create metric filters. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Logs — centralised log collection with retention, metric filters
Amazon S3 alone — durable object storage that can hold log files but lacks built-in retention policies
Amazon QuickSight — business-intelligence dashboards on top of curated datasets
AWS Snowball — petabyte-scale offline data transfer device
questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs centralizes logs from any source. You can create metric filters (count errors in logs), set alarms, and analyze with CloudWatch Logs Insights queries. The other options are incorrect: Amazon S3 alone — durable object storage that can hold log files but lacks built-in retention policies, metric filters, and live tailing without extra services. Amazon QuickSight — business-intelligence dashboards on top of curated datasets; it does not natively collect logs from EC2, Lambda, or VPC sources. AWS Snowball — petabyte-scale offline data transfer device; not a managed live log-collection service for EC2, Lambda, or VPC sources.

questions.question: An architect designing for high availability must distinguish two AWS scope concepts: (1) a geographic area containing multiple isolated data-centre clusters connected by low-latency fibre, (2) one or more of those data-centre clusters in distinct power/cooling/network failure domains. Which mapping is correct?
options: Both Region and AZ are interchangeable labels for the same physical datacentre
A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones
A Region is a load-balancer pool and an AZ is the IP subnet managed by that pool
A Region is a marketing label with no physical separation between its AZs
questions.explanation: A Region (e.g., us-east-1) is a geographic cluster of AZs. An AZ (e.g., us-east-1a) is one or more data centers with independent infrastructure. Multi-AZ deployments protect against single data center failure. The other options are incorrect: Both Region and AZ are interchangeable labels for the same physical datacentre — false; a Region is a geographic area grouping multiple Availability Zones each with independent power and cooling infrastructure. A Region is a load-balancer pool and an AZ is the IP subnet managed by that pool — false; a Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated AZs, not a load-balancing construct. A Region is a marketing label with no physical separation between its AZs — false; a Region is a real geographic area whose multiple AZs are physically isolated facilities.
