questions.question: A backend team builds 30 REST and WebSocket endpoints. They want a managed service that handles: throttling, API keys, usage plans, JWT auth, request/response mapping, canary deployments, and CloudFront-edge presence. Which AWS service?
options: An on-prem network gateway device — a physical appliance
Amazon CloudFront — CDN for caching HTTP responses at edge locations
Amazon Route 53 — DNS resolution and domain registration
Amazon API Gateway — managed REST + WebSocket API front end
questions.explanation: API Gateway is the front door for backend services (Lambda, EC2, HTTP endpoints). It handles authentication, throttling, caching, monitoring, versioning, and API key management. The other options are incorrect: An on-prem network gateway device — a physical appliance; not a managed AWS service that handles REST request/response routing, throttling, or WebSocket connection mapping. Amazon CloudFront — CDN for caching HTTP responses at edge locations; it does not provide REST API keys, usage plans, canary deployments, JWT auth, or request/response mapping for backend service endpoints. Amazon Route 53 — DNS resolution and domain registration; it maps domain names to endpoints but does not manage individual API request/response routing, throttling, or WebSocket protocol handling.

questions.question: A backend must orchestrate this flow: (1) start a Lambda, (2) wait for human approval, (3) run a Glue ETL job, (4) on success notify SNS, (5) on failure invoke a different Lambda. The flow is long-running, has retries with exponential backoff, and is auditable. Which service?
options: AWS Lambda chained directly with synchronous invocations only — possible but lacks built-in state
Amazon SQS alone — provides reliable queueing primitives but no built-in orchestration, branching
AWS Step Functions — managed state-machine workflow orchestrator with built-in retries, branching
Amazon EventBridge alone — event bus that routes events between services but offers no built-in retries
questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates distributed applications as state machines with visual workflows. Coordinates Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SNS, SQS, and more with built-in error handling and retries. The other options are incorrect: AWS Lambda chained directly with synchronous invocations only — possible but lacks built-in state tracking, automatic retries, and visual workflow representation for the steps. Amazon SQS alone — provides reliable queueing primitives but no built-in orchestration, branching, or visual representation of multi-step workflow logic. Amazon EventBridge alone — event bus that routes events between services but offers no built-in retries, branching, or visual orchestration of a multi-step workflow.

questions.question: An architect maps a workload's improvement to one of the six Well-Architected pillars. The work focuses on rightsizing instance families, buying Savings Plans, deleting idle resources, lifecycle-tiering S3. Which pillar?
options: Operational Excellence — focused on operations process improvements such as automation and runbook quality
Cost Optimisation — rightsizing, RIs/SP, eliminating idle, tier-by-access
Reliability — focused on recovery from failure and fault tolerance
Performance Efficiency — using the right resources efficiently for performance requirements
questions.explanation: Cost Optimization pillar focuses on avoiding unnecessary costs: right-sizing instances, using Reserved/Spot pricing, deleting unused resources, and understanding spend. All 6 pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability. The other options are incorrect: Operational Excellence — focused on operations process improvements such as automation and runbook quality; not the pillar that addresses idle resource elimination and rightsizing cost. Reliability — focused on recovery from failure and fault tolerance; not the pillar that covers idle resource elimination, rightsizing, and cost optimisation. Performance Efficiency — using the right resources efficiently for performance requirements; adjacent to cost but not the pillar that explicitly addresses idle resource elimination and rightsizing.

questions.question: An app must retrieve an RDS password at runtime that auto-rotates every 30 days, encrypts at rest with a customer-managed KMS key, and emits a CloudTrail event on each retrieval. Which AWS service stores and rotates this secret?
options: Browser-based consumer password manager — designed for human credential storage and copy-paste retrieval
S3 default encryption — encrypts objects at rest with a configured key
IAM password policy — governs the format and rotation of IAM user console passwords
AWS Secrets Manager — KMS-encrypted secret store with built-in rotation
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets securely and can automatically rotate them (e.g., RDS passwords every 30 days) without application downtime. Applications retrieve secrets via API — no hardcoded credentials. The other options are incorrect: Browser-based consumer password manager — designed for human credential storage and copy-paste retrieval; it does not integrate with CloudTrail for audit logging, provide programmatic SDKs, or auto-rotate secrets. S3 default encryption — encrypts objects at rest with a configured key; it is not a key/value secret store with programmatic retrieval or built-in rotation for application credentials. IAM password policy — governs the format and rotation of IAM user console passwords; it does not store or provide programmatic retrieval of application secrets like database credentials.

questions.question: An architect new to AWS asks where to find AWS's prescriptive best-practice guidance, organised into pillars that an architecture review can score against (with detailed lenses for serverless, machine-learning, SaaS, IoT). Which official AWS resource is this?
options: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party software and SaaS listings for purchase
AWS Well-Architected Framework — six pillars plus domain-specific lenses with prescriptive
AWS Service Catalog — lets internal admins curate approved CloudFormation templates for end users
AWS Solutions Library — pre-built reference implementations for common workloads
questions.explanation: The Well-Architected Framework helps architects build secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient infrastructure. Use the Well-Architected Tool in the AWS console for free architectural reviews. The other options are incorrect: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party software and SaaS listings for purchase; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance. AWS Service Catalog — lets internal admins curate approved CloudFormation templates for end users; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance. AWS Solutions Library — pre-built reference implementations for common workloads; useful examples, but not the canonical place for AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars and lenses.

questions.question: A team wants to run ad-hoc SQL queries DIRECTLY against parquet/CSV/JSON files stored in S3, with NO database to provision, billed per TB scanned. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS — managed relational database
Amazon Athena — serverless interactive SQL directly over parquet/CSV/JSON files
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves databases between engines and to AWS
AWS Glue — managed ETL service whose Data Catalog integrates with Athena
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over data in S3 using Presto/Trino. Billed per TB scanned. Uses the Glue Data Catalog. DMS is a migration tool. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS — managed relational database; data must be loaded into the engine before SQL queries can run directly; it is not billed per-query-scanned for ad-hoc analysis. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves databases between engines and to AWS; it does not run SQL queries directly against parquet/CSV/JSON files or bill per data scanned. AWS Glue — managed ETL service whose Data Catalog integrates with Athena; Glue itself runs ETL jobs and is billed per DPU-hour, not by the data directly scanned per query.

questions.question: A team wants a managed ETL service to (a) crawl source data, build a data catalog with schemas, (b) author and run Spark / Python jobs that transform S3 / RDS / Redshift data, (c) all serverless. Which AWS service?
options: VPC Reachability Analyzer — a networking diagnostic tool
AWS CodePipeline — a managed CI/CD pipeline for software delivery
AWS Glue — serverless ETL with Crawlers + Data Catalog + Spark/Python jobs
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — a real-time streaming primitive for event ingest
questions.explanation: AWS Glue provides: Data Catalog (metadata repository for all your data sources), ETL jobs (serverless Spark-based transformations), and Crawlers (auto-discover schema from S3, RDS, etc.). The other options are incorrect: VPC Reachability Analyzer — a networking diagnostic tool; it is not a serverless ETL service and does not run Spark or Python jobs or build a data catalog. AWS CodePipeline — a managed CI/CD pipeline for software delivery; it does not provide serverless Spark/Python ETL jobs or a crawler-based data catalog. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — a real-time streaming primitive for event ingest; it is not a serverless batch ETL service and does not run Spark or Python crawling jobs.

questions.question: A team wants to run Docker workloads with AWS-native orchestration (no Kubernetes). They want to pick the underlying compute: either EC2 (customer-managed) or Fargate (serverless). Which AWS service is the orchestrator?
options: Amazon ECS — AWS-native container orchestrator
Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane for running Docker workloads
Amazon ECR — managed container image registry for Docker and OCI images
EC2 Auto Scaling Group — scales VM compute capacity horizontally
questions.explanation: ECS manages containerized applications. EC2 launch type: you manage the underlying EC2 fleet. Fargate: serverless — no EC2 management. Amazon ECR stores container images. ECS integrates with ALB, IAM, CloudWatch. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane for running Docker workloads; you choose either self-managed node groups or AWS-managed nodes, but this is Kubernetes-based, not the AWS-native ECS orchestrator. Amazon ECR — managed container image registry for Docker and OCI images; it is not a container orchestrator and provides no customer compute or scheduling capability. EC2 Auto Scaling Group — scales VM compute capacity horizontally; it is not a container orchestrator and does not support Fargate serverless task execution or ECS task-definition scheduling.

questions.question: A pre-baked OS image with a specific Linux distro, kernel version, pre-installed nginx + Python venv, and security-hardened config is published as a reusable EC2 image. Launching a new EC2 from this image gives you that EXACT environment. What is this template called?
options: AWS Management Console — browser-based admin UI for AWS
An Amazon Machine Image — template that EC2 uses to provision new instances
An asymmetric key-pair — used to SSH into a Linux instance after launch
A VPC template — defines a virtual network (CIDR, subnets, route tables)
questions.explanation: An AMI is the EC2 launch template: it bundles a root volume snapshot, launch permissions, and a block-device mapping. AMI ≠ the browser management console. The other options are incorrect: AWS Management Console — browser-based admin UI for AWS; not the pre-baked OS image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software. An asymmetric key-pair — used to SSH into a Linux instance after launch; not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software. A VPC template — defines a virtual network (CIDR, subnets, route tables); not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software.

questions.question: A SOC engineer needs the AUTHORITATIVE record of every API call against the AWS account: who (principal), what (action), when (timestamp), from where (IP, user-agent), with what (request parameters), result (status). The service is tenant-wide and immutable by default. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer — diagnoses network-path reachability between source and destination
AWS CloudTrail — tenant-wide, immutable, default-on log of every AWS API call with caller identity
Amazon CloudWatch Logs — general application and system log aggregation
VPC Flow Logs — captures IP traffic flow records for every network interface
questions.explanation: CloudTrail is the tenant-wide audit log of AWS API calls. CloudWatch Logs aggregates application/system logs but is NOT the API audit trail. The other options are incorrect: Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer — diagnoses network-path reachability between source and destination; it does not record every API call, tenant-wide user identity, request timestamp, or immutable audit history. Amazon CloudWatch Logs — general application and system log aggregation; it does not capture every AWS API call, tenant-wide immutable event history, or per-request user agent and timestamp by default. VPC Flow Logs — captures IP traffic flow records for every network interface; it does not record every AWS API call, user identity, request parameters, or tenant-wide control-plane audit events.

questions.question: An IaC team compares two AWS provisioning tools: (A) declarative templates in YAML or JSON; resources, parameters, mappings, outputs. (B) imperative TypeScript / Python / Java / Go / .NET code that SYNTHESISES into (A)'s template format. Which is which?
options: AWS CloudFormation is declarative; AWS CDK is imperative-feeling — define stacks
CloudFormation uses imperative scripts and CDK uses declarative YAML templates
Both CloudFormation and CDK are declarative-only YAML tools with no TypeScript or Java support
CloudFormation requires JSON-only and CDK requires Python-only
questions.explanation: CloudFormation is the foundational IaC service — template-based. CDK allows writing infrastructure using familiar languages with OOP constructs, then synthesizes CloudFormation. Higher level of abstraction. The other options are incorrect: CloudFormation uses imperative scripts and CDK uses declarative YAML templates — reversed; CloudFormation uses declarative YAML/JSON templates while CDK generates them from imperative TypeScript, Python, Java, and other languages. Both CloudFormation and CDK are declarative-only YAML tools with no TypeScript or Java support — false; CDK supports TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go as imperative languages that generate the declarative templates. CloudFormation requires JSON-only and CDK requires Python-only — false; CloudFormation accepts both JSON and YAML templates; CDK supports TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go.

questions.question: An IAM principal is granted `s3:GetObject` by an attached identity policy AND explicitly denied `s3:GetObject` by a resource policy on the same bucket. AWS's IAM evaluation logic says one rule about Allow vs Deny is absolute. Which is it?
options: The request is allowed because IAM identity-based allow grants always override resource-based deny
The request is denied because IAM evaluation logic dictates that an explicit deny in any policy
The request is allowed because S3 bucket-policy denials only apply to anonymous unauthenticated
The request is denied because S3 GetObject always requires an MFA token evaluated through the IAM
questions.explanation: AWS IAM policy evaluation: Any explicit Deny wins regardless of any Allow. This enables denying specific actions even for admins. All requests start as implicitly denied — Allows must be explicitly granted. The other options are incorrect: The request is allowed because IAM identity-based allow grants always override resource-based deny policies in the IAM evaluation logic — false; an explicit deny in any IAM policy type overrides any allow in the evaluation logic. The request is allowed because S3 bucket-policy denials only apply to anonymous unauthenticated requests in the IAM evaluation logic — false; bucket-policy explicit denies apply to all principals regardless of authentication in the IAM evaluation logic. The request is denied because S3 GetObject always requires an MFA token evaluated through the IAM request condition logic — false; MFA is not required by default; the deny here comes from the explicit deny in the resource-based policy evaluation logic.

questions.question: A company moves 8 Gbps of sustained traffic between an on-prem DC and AWS. They need (a) consistent, predictable throughput (not best-effort internet), (b) lower egress pricing than internet, (c) data must NOT traverse the public internet. Which AWS service?
options: A site-to-site VPN over the public internet — an encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS
AWS Direct Connect — dedicated private network link between on-prem
AWS Snowball Edge — a petabyte-scale offline physical transfer device for bulk data migration
Amazon CloudFront — a global CDN for cached HTTP content delivery
questions.explanation: Direct Connect provides 1Gbps or 10Gbps dedicated connections via AWS Direct Connect Partners. Unlike VPN, no internet fluctuations. Good for large data transfers, hybrid cloud, and compliance requirements. The other options are incorrect: A site-to-site VPN over the public internet — an encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS; it traverses shared public internet links with unpredictable latency and no guaranteed bandwidth SLA. AWS Snowball Edge — a petabyte-scale offline physical transfer device for bulk data migration; it provides no ongoing predictable network connectivity for sustained 8 Gbps traffic. Amazon CloudFront — a global CDN for cached HTTP content delivery; it provides edge caching but no dedicated predictable private circuit for sustained high-bandwidth on-prem connectivity.

questions.question: A team needs a HIERARCHICAL key/value config + secret store for app config: dev/prod/region scoping via the path key, AT REST encryption via KMS for SecureString entries, version history per parameter, and a generous free tier. Which AWS service fits (without Secrets Manager's automatic rotation features)?
options: AWS Secrets Manager — supports rotation and KMS encryption for secrets
S3 bucket storing config files — works for configuration but has no native KMS SecureString tier
EC2 fleet manager operations — manages instance patching and sessions
Systems Manager Parameter Store — hierarchical, KMS-encrypted SecureString, version history
questions.explanation: Parameter Store stores config data (DB strings, feature flags, AMI IDs) hierarchically (e.g., /prod/db/password). Free for standard parameters. SecureString type encrypts with KMS. Alternative to hardcoded config. The other options are incorrect: AWS Secrets Manager — supports rotation and KMS encryption for secrets; it is a paid service charged per secret rather than the free standard-tier hierarchical store suited for plain app configuration. S3 bucket storing config files — works for configuration but has no native KMS SecureString tier, hierarchical parameter path lookup, or built-in version history for individual keys. EC2 fleet manager operations — manages instance patching and sessions; it does not provide hierarchical parameter storage, SecureString tier, or version history for configuration values.

questions.question: An e-commerce service needs a NoSQL database with: (a) single-digit ms latency at any scale, (b) no servers to provision, (c) horizontal partitioning by item key, (d) global tables (multi-region active-active), (e) on-demand or provisioned capacity. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS for MySQL — relational engine with single-region read replicas
Amazon DynamoDB with Global Tables — managed NoSQL key-value store
Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale analytical data warehouse for OLAP workloads
Amazon ElastiCache — in-memory cache (Redis/Memcached)
questions.explanation: DynamoDB: zero administration, auto-scales from 0 to millions of requests/second. Single-digit millisecond latency. Choose when: high throughput, flexible schema, simple queries by primary key. Not ideal for complex joins. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS for MySQL — relational engine with single-region read replicas; lacks single-digit-millisecond NoSQL semantics and global multi-region active-active replication. Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale analytical data warehouse for OLAP workloads; not a NoSQL store with single-digit-millisecond latency for transactional reads. Amazon ElastiCache — in-memory cache (Redis/Memcached); fast but volatile, single-region, and not a durable NoSQL store with multi-region Global Tables replication.

questions.question: A first Lambda invocation after a long idle period shows 800 ms of added latency. The next invocation a second later finishes in 30 ms. The 800-ms first-hit overhead is documented as the time to provision a new execution environment, download the deployment package, start the runtime, and run any module-level init. Which Lambda phenomenon is this?
options: Region cold start — a hypothetical one-time environment provisioning event that would affect all
Billing first-invocation surcharge
Cold start — execution-environment provisioning, runtime load
Execution timeout — a hard limit that terminates a too-long invocation at the END of its runtime
questions.explanation: Lambda cold start = time to provision container + load runtime + init your code. Mitigation: Provisioned Concurrency (keeps environments warm), Lambda SnapStart (Java), smaller deployment packages, faster runtimes (Node/Python vs Java). The other options are incorrect: Region cold start — a hypothetical one-time environment provisioning event that would affect all invocations across the Region simultaneously after a long idle period; not an invocation-specific init latency spike. Billing first-invocation surcharge — not a real Lambda billing item; Lambda bills per request and duration; the startup latency is a cold start init event, not a billing surcharge. Execution timeout — a hard limit that terminates a too-long invocation at the END of its runtime; not the added init and runtime provisioning latency at the start of a cold invocation.

questions.question: A network team is connecting 10 VPCs. With VPC Peering each pair needs its own peer (a full mesh = 45 peerings) AND traffic is not transitive (A→B→C does not work via two peerings). With one alternative service the team creates one hub and N spoke attachments, with transitive routing between any spokes. Which two services and which difference?
options: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway are interchangeable
Transit Gateway is the legacy product that VPC Peering replaced
VPC Peering = non-transitive 1:1 link; Transit Gateway = transitive hub-and-spoke for many VPCs
VPC Peering supports more VPC attachments per hub than Transit Gateway
questions.explanation: VPC Peering: simple, low-cost, no transitive routing (A↔B and B↔C doesn't mean A↔C). Transit Gateway: scalable hub for 1000s of VPCs and VPNs with transitive routing, route tables, and multicast support. The other options are incorrect: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway are interchangeable — false; Peering creates non-transitive 1:1 links between two VPCs only, while Transit Gateway connects thousands of VPCs in a hub-and-spoke transitive topology. Transit Gateway is the legacy product that VPC Peering replaced — false; Transit Gateway is the newer hub-and-spoke service with transitive routing; VPC Peering is the older 1:1 non-transitive link primitive. VPC Peering supports more VPC attachments per hub than Transit Gateway — false; Transit Gateway supports thousands of VPC attachments while VPC Peering is limited to bilateral 1:1 non-transitive connections between individual VPC pairs.

questions.question: A compliance archive of CT scan images must be retained 30 years. Access frequency is well below 1 read per year. Retrieval latency may be 12 hours. Minimum storage cost is the only optimisation criterion. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive — lowest per-GB cost, multi-hour retrieval, ideal for 30-yr cold archive
S3 Standard — the most expensive per-GB storage class with millisecond retrieval
S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers objects based on access patterns but adds a per-object monitoring cost
S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent-access storage at a lower cost than Standard
questions.explanation: S3 storage classes by access frequency: Standard > Intelligent-Tiering > Standard-IA > One Zone-IA > Glacier Instant > Glacier Flexible Retrieval > Glacier Deep Archive. Match access pattern to class to minimize costs. The other options are incorrect: S3 Standard — the most expensive per-GB storage class with millisecond retrieval; not appropriate for a 30-year archive with infrequent access where cost efficiency is the primary driver. S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers objects based on access patterns but adds a per-object monitoring cost; the access pattern here is known and rare enough that Deep Archive's lower cost wins. S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent-access storage at a lower cost than Standard; it has a higher per-GB cost than Deep Archive and lacks multi-AZ redundancy for a 30-year retention requirement.

questions.question: An operations engineer wants to scale capacity based on demand for: (a) EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group, (b) DynamoDB read/write capacity, (c) ECS service desired-count, (d) Aurora read replicas. AWS offers a unified service that orchestrates scaling across all of these. Which?
options: Auto Scaling is only available for EC2
AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing of EC2, EBS, and Lambda based on usage history
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes incoming requests across registered targets
AWS Auto Scaling — orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASG, DynamoDB, ECS
questions.explanation: Auto Scaling policies: Target Tracking (e.g., CPU at 70%), Step Scaling (add 2 instances when CPU > 80%), Scheduled Scaling (predict load). Scaling out = add instances, Scaling in = remove instances. The other options are incorrect: Auto Scaling is only available for EC2 — false; AWS Auto Scaling orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASGs, DynamoDB tables, Aurora replicas, ECS services, and Lambda provisioned concurrency. AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing of EC2, EBS, and Lambda based on usage history; it does not orchestrate live scaling or automatically adjust capacity in real time. Elastic Load Balancing — distributes incoming requests across registered targets; it does not orchestrate or auto-scale the backend capacity that handles those requests.

questions.question: A security team wants automated, continuous scans of resource-based policies (S3 buckets, KMS keys, IAM roles, Lambda) to find resources shared EXTERNALLY (with other AWS accounts, public internet, federated principals). Findings are categorised as 'expected sharing' vs 'unintended exposure'. Which AWS service?
options: IAM Password Auditor
IAM Policy Generator wizard — a console tool that helps authors compose JSON policies
IAM Access Analyzer — continuously analyses resource-based policies on S3, KMS
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecast across accounts
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to find S3 buckets, KMS keys, Lambda functions, IAM roles, and SQS queues that are accessible from outside your AWS account — reducing data exposure risk. The other options are incorrect: IAM Password Auditor — no canonical AWS service with this name; password policy auditing is a Trusted Advisor check that does not analyse resource-based policies on S3 buckets, Lambda functions, or shared roles. IAM Policy Generator wizard — a console tool that helps authors compose JSON policies; it does not continuously analyse existing resource-based policies on S3, Lambda, or shared role trust relationships. AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecast across accounts; it does not analyse resource-based policies on S3, Lambda, or externally shared role trust configurations.

questions.question: A vendor's SaaS service runs in their AWS account. Our security team requires our VPC to consume that service over PRIVATE IPs on the AWS backbone, NOT via the public internet, without site-to-site VPN. Which service enables this private cross-account/cross-service consumption pattern?
options: AWS Client VPN — managed remote-user VPN endpoint for client-to-VPC connectivity
S3 Access Points — bucket-level constructs that scope IAM policies for S3 access
AWS PrivateLink — interface endpoints in our VPC privately consume the vendor's endpoint service
Direct Connect virtual interfaces — provide private on-prem-to-AWS connectivity without the public internet
questions.explanation: PrivateLink creates private endpoints in your VPC for AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, CloudWatch) or third-party SaaS services. Traffic stays on AWS network — no internet exposure, no NAT gateway costs for AWS service traffic. The other options are incorrect: AWS Client VPN — managed remote-user VPN endpoint for client-to-VPC connectivity; it does not allow our VPC to consume a vendor's endpoint service over the AWS backbone without traversing the public internet. S3 Access Points — bucket-level constructs that scope IAM policies for S3 access; they do not create VPC interface endpoints for privately consuming external vendor services without public internet exposure. Direct Connect virtual interfaces — provide private on-prem-to-AWS connectivity without the public internet; they do not create VPC-side interface endpoints for consuming services in another vendor's AWS account privately.

questions.question: A finance team wants to be alerted when AWS spend hits 50%, 80%, and 100% of the monthly budget. The control must also support automatic actions (e.g., stop EC2 instances, apply an IAM policy) on threshold breach. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Cost Explorer alerts only — provides historical and forecast charts
AWS Budgets — set monthly cost or usage budgets at 50/80/100% thresholds with email/SNS alerts
AWS Trusted Advisor budget module — surfaces cost-optimisation checks but does not directly emit
Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms only — fires on metrics like CPU
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets lets you define cost/usage/RI coverage budgets with SNS email/SMS alerts. Budget Actions can automatically apply IAM policies or stop EC2/RDS instances when thresholds are crossed. The other options are incorrect: AWS Cost Explorer alerts only — provides historical and forecast charts but cannot directly trigger budget-driven email or automated stop-EC2 actions at thresholds. AWS Trusted Advisor budget module — surfaces cost-optimisation checks but does not directly emit threshold alerts at 50/80/100% or apply policy actions. Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms only — fires on metrics like CPU; supports custom cost metrics but is not the canonical AWS service for monthly cost budgets and actions.

questions.question: A global service needs DNS routing that, on a per-record basis, can: route by latency to closest Region, fail over from primary to secondary on health-check fail, weight requests across blue/green deployments, geofence answers by user country, and return multiple answers with health-aware selection. Which AWS DNS service provides ALL of these routing policies?
options: Route 53 supports only a single simple round-robin policy across all records
Route 53 routing policies apply only to Alias records
Route 53 supports: Simple, Weighted, Latency-based
Route 53 routing is scoped to EC2-only targets
questions.explanation: Route 53 routing policies enable sophisticated DNS-based traffic management: Weighted for canary deployments, Latency-based for global performance, Failover for disaster recovery, Geolocation for compliance/localization. The other options are incorrect: Route 53 supports only a single simple round-robin policy across all records — false; Route 53 supports per-record basis policies including Latency, Geolocation, Failover, Weighted, and IP-based routing. Route 53 routing policies apply only to Alias records — false; routing policies apply to both Alias and non-Alias (CNAME/A) records; latency-based, geolocation, and weighted routing work on either. Route 53 routing is scoped to EC2-only targets — false; Route 53 routing-policy targets include ALBs, CloudFront distributions, S3 websites, IP addresses, and any DNS-resolvable endpoint, not just EC2.

questions.question: Two IAM policy categories sit alongside in an account: one is AUTHORED, NUMBERED, and maintained by AWS (e.g., AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess), the other is AUTHORED by the customer (e.g., MyAppReadOnly). The first is automatically updated when AWS adds new permissions; the second is the customer's responsibility. Which is which?
options: AWS Managed policies are pre-built, AWS-maintained
AWS Managed and Customer Managed policies behave identically at IAM evaluation
Customer Managed policies are inherently less secure than AWS Managed policies
AWS Managed policies can only attach to IAM users
questions.explanation: AWS Managed Policies: maintained by AWS, updated automatically when services change, reusable. Customer Managed: you control content, version history, can apply fine-grained permissions. Inline policies: embedded in a single identity. The other options are incorrect: AWS Managed and Customer Managed policies behave identically at IAM evaluation — false; AWS Managed policies are AWS-authored and AWS-maintained with version tracking, while Customer Managed policies are customer-authored and customer-maintained. Customer Managed policies are inherently less secure than AWS Managed policies — false; security depends on policy content; AWS-authored managed policies follow best practices but Customer Managed policies can be equally secure when properly authored. AWS Managed policies can only attach to IAM users — false; AWS-maintained managed policies attach to users, groups, and roles; attaching them to roles is the most common pattern for EC2 and Lambda.

questions.question: A media site's static assets must be delivered with sub-50 ms latency to users in 50 countries. The service must cache GETs at global edge POPs, terminate TLS at the edge, and integrate with WAF + Shield. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Elemental MediaPackage — video packaging and origin service for static and live streaming media
AWS WAF — Layer-7 web-firewall rules engine
Amazon Route 53 — DNS service with latency-based routing
Amazon CloudFront — global CDN with 600+ edge POPs, edge TLS termination, WAF and Shield integration
questions.explanation: CloudFront caches static and dynamic content at edge locations. Reduces origin load and latency for global users. Supports Lambda@Edge for edge compute, signed URLs/cookies for private content, and AWS WAF integration. The other options are incorrect: AWS Elemental MediaPackage — video packaging and origin service for static and live streaming media; it is not a CDN with global edge POPs and static-asset Shield-integrated delivery. AWS WAF — Layer-7 web-firewall rules engine; it complements a CDN but is not itself the static-asset delivery network with global POPs and Shield DDoS integration. Amazon Route 53 — DNS service with latency-based routing; it resolves names to endpoints but is not a CDN with global edge POPs that caches and delivers static assets.

questions.question: An architect needs to forecast the monthly cost of a PROPOSED architecture (Lambda + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront + Route 53) BEFORE deploying anything. The tool must use AWS list prices and produce a per-service breakdown. Which AWS tool?
options: AWS Bills — shows past monthly spend by account, service, and tag for charges already incurred
AWS Invoice Manager — handles invoicing for AWS Organizations payers
AWS Cost Saver Report
AWS Pricing Calculator — free web tool that estimates monthly cost for proposed architectures
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws.amazon.com) helps estimate costs upfront. Model EC2 instance types, storage, data transfer, and other services to build a cost estimate for budget approval or comparison. The other options are incorrect: AWS Bills — shows past monthly spend by account, service, and tag for charges already incurred; it is not a pre-deployment pricing tool for estimating a proposed architecture's future cost. AWS Invoice Manager — handles invoicing for AWS Organizations payers; it is not a tool for estimating future prices or modelling proposed deployment costs. AWS Cost Saver Report — not a documented AWS product; no canonical AWS tool uses that name for estimating deployment prices.

questions.question: An organisation considers AWS Support plans. The free tier covers billing-only. Above that there are three paid tiers offering increasing response-time SLAs and channels (email vs phone vs TAM). Which describes the four tiers correctly?
options: Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp / Enterprise
Every AWS support plan includes 24×7 phone response and an assigned TAM regardless of billing tier
Every AWS support plan includes an assigned TAM regardless of billing plan
Enterprise Support is free once monthly billing crosses a spending threshold
questions.explanation: Support plan tiers: Basic (free) → Developer → Business → Enterprise On-Ramp → Enterprise. Business and above get: 24/7 phone support, full Trusted Advisor checks, and access to Infrastructure Event Management. The other options are incorrect: Every AWS support plan includes 24×7 phone response and an assigned TAM regardless of billing tier — false; 24×7 phone response is only available on Business and Enterprise plans, and TAM access is Enterprise-only. Every AWS support plan includes an assigned TAM regardless of billing plan — false; TAM access is exclusive to Enterprise support; Developer and Business plans have email or chat support without a named TAM. Enterprise Support is free once monthly billing crosses a spending threshold — false; Enterprise Support has a separate paid subscription fee based on monthly AWS billing, not a free tier.

questions.question: An app must send 2 million transactional emails per month (purchase receipts, account-verification, password-reset) with a managed deliverability service, no SMTP server to operate. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch — operational metrics and log aggregation surface
Amazon GuardDuty — security threat-detection service for AWS API and VPC Flow logs
Amazon SES — managed transactional and marketing email sending at scale
Amazon WorkMail — managed business email mailboxes for end users
questions.explanation: SES sends emails from applications (order confirmations, password resets, newsletters). Integrates with Lambda and SNS. Handles bounce/complaint processing. Can also receive emails and trigger Lambda functions. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudWatch — operational metrics and log aggregation surface; not a managed transactional email-sending service with deliverability and SMTP/REST endpoints. Amazon GuardDuty — security threat-detection service for AWS API and VPC Flow logs; not a managed transactional email-sending service with deliverability. Amazon WorkMail — managed business email mailboxes for end users; targets desktop mail clients rather than high-volume transactional email from applications.

questions.question: Security best practice in IAM says: a new IAM principal should START WITH ZERO permissions; permissions are added on a documented need-to-do basis; periodic audit removes unused permissions. Which principle is this?
options: Grant administrator permissions broadly to avoid friction during onboarding — the opposite of least
Grant broad read permissions to every principal by default and tighten unused permissions later
Least Privilege — grant the minimum permissions required; start with none
Apply least privilege only to IAM users and exempt IAM roles from the documented minimum permissions
questions.explanation: Least privilege: users, roles, and services should have only the exact permissions they need. Use IAM Access Advisor to see last used permissions. Remove unused permissions. Prefer managed policies over wildcard (*) actions. The other options are incorrect: Grant administrator permissions broadly to avoid friction during onboarding — the opposite of least privilege; broad permissions are harder to audit and create unnecessary risk beyond documented need. Grant broad read permissions to every principal by default and tighten unused permissions later — false; least privilege means starting with no permissions, not starting broad and removing unused grants. Apply least privilege only to IAM users and exempt IAM roles from the documented minimum permissions requirement — false; least privilege applies to all IAM principals including roles, service accounts, and federated identities.

questions.question: A team needs MANAGED file systems for specific protocols: SMB for Windows file shares, Lustre for high-performance computing, NetApp ONTAP for migration from on-prem ONTAP, OpenZFS for ZFS workloads. They want one AWS service family that covers all four. Which?
options: A new EBS volume type — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance
Amazon FSx — managed file-system family that covers each of those
Amazon EFS — managed NFS (NFSv4) file system only
AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as an on-prem file and tape gateway
questions.explanation: FSx is the managed file-systems family: Windows File Server (SMB), Lustre (HPC), NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS. Storage Gateway is different (hybrid). The other options are incorrect: A new EBS volume type — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance; it does not cover managed protocol-specific file systems for SMB, Lustre, or NetApp ONTAP workloads. Amazon EFS — managed NFS (NFSv4) file system only; it does not cover the SMB, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS protocols offered by the FSx managed file-system family. AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as an on-prem file and tape gateway; it covers only on-prem bridge scenarios and does not provide cloud-native Windows SMB shares, Lustre HPC, or ONTAP managed by FSx.

questions.question: An on-prem NAS holds 200 TB of files that must be migrated INCREMENTALLY (initial bulk + ongoing deltas) to Amazon S3 and EFS. The team wants a managed service with bandwidth throttling, encryption in transit, scheduling, and integrity verification — without writing custom scripts. Which service?
options: AWS DMS — managed database migration service for engine-to-engine schema and data transfer
RDS read-replica — asynchronously replicates a primary RDS database for read scaling
DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-region active-active replication for DynamoDB tables
AWS DataSync — managed online file/object data-transfer accelerator with scheduling
questions.explanation: DataSync automates and accelerates data migration/sync. Uses a DataSync Agent on-premises. Handles scheduling, monitoring, encryption, and data validation. Ideal for one-time migrations or ongoing data processing workflows. The other options are incorrect: AWS DMS — managed database migration service for engine-to-engine schema and data transfer; it does not perform incremental file-level scheduling, transfer throttling, or integrity verification for NAS migration. RDS read-replica — asynchronously replicates a primary RDS database for read scaling; it does not migrate NAS file data or support incremental scheduling and integrity verification for file transfers. DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-region active-active replication for DynamoDB tables; it does not migrate on-prem NAS file data or provide transfer scheduling, throttling, or file integrity verification.

questions.question: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, for a Lambda function deployed in customer code, who is responsible for: (a) hypervisor patching, (b) Lambda runtime (e.g., python3.12) patching, (c) the customer's function CODE, (d) the IAM role attached, (e) the data the function reads/writes?
options: Customer owns the Lambda runtime and underlying OS
Customer handles only OS patching for Lambda
Lambda is identical to EC2 in the Shared Responsibility Model
AWS handles infrastructure, OS, and runtime patching
questions.explanation: Serverless shifts more responsibility to AWS. For Lambda, you don't manage: servers, OS, runtime patches, capacity. You still own: your code, IAM roles, data encryption, network access, and application-level security. The other options are incorrect: Customer owns the Lambda runtime and underlying OS — false; AWS manages and patches the Lambda runtime, operating system, and underlying compute; the customer owns the function code, IAM role, and data. Customer handles only OS patching for Lambda — false; AWS handles OS patching; the customer is responsible for the function code, the IAM role permissions, and the data processed by the function. Lambda is identical to EC2 in the Shared Responsibility Model — false; Lambda is more managed than EC2; on EC2 customers own OS patching and runtime; on Lambda those responsibilities shift to AWS, leaving the customer responsible for function code, IAM role, and data.

questions.question: A web/mobile app needs a managed identity service for END USERS (not AWS administrators). Requirements: user sign-up / sign-in with email or social login (Google, Facebook), MFA, password-reset, and a federated path to obtain AWS credentials for direct service calls. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS — managed relational database service for application data
AWS IAM — identity management for AWS administrators and workloads inside the account
Amazon Cognito — User Pools plus Identity Pools for end users of a web or mobile app
AWS Client VPN — managed remote-access VPN authentication endpoint
questions.explanation: Cognito User Pools: user directory, handles sign-up/sign-in, MFA, OAuth2. Identity Pools (Federated Identities): swap tokens from social providers (Google, Facebook) or User Pools for temporary AWS credentials. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS — managed relational database service for application data; it does not provide identity management for end users, federated sign-in, or temporary credentials for mobile app authentication. AWS IAM — identity management for AWS administrators and workloads inside the account; it is not designed for managing millions of end users or providing federated social-login credentials for consumer applications. AWS Client VPN — managed remote-access VPN authentication endpoint; it handles device-level VPN credentials, not end-user identity management, federation, or application-tier temporary credentials.

questions.question: A company has Oracle, SQL Server, and Windows Server licences they own (BYOL). They want a managed inventory tool that tracks each license, attaches them to AWS / on-prem instances, and alerts when a deployment would exceed the licence count. Which AWS service?
options: AWS License Manager — manages BYOL licences across AWS and on-prem fleets
AWS Marketplace — catalogue for buying third-party AMIs and SaaS subscriptions
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecasts
AWS Resource Groups — groups arbitrary AWS resources by tag for batch operations
questions.explanation: License Manager helps track BYOL (Bring Your Own License) software deployments on EC2, prevents launching instances that would violate license terms, and provides a centralized dashboard for license inventory. The other options are incorrect: AWS Marketplace — catalogue for buying third-party AMIs and SaaS subscriptions; it does not manage BYOL licence counts, track on-prem installations, or enforce per-instance licence seat limits. AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecasts; it does not track BYOL software licences, enforce per-seat license limits, or flag overuse across on-prem and cloud fleets. AWS Resource Groups — groups arbitrary AWS resources by tag for batch operations; it does not track software licence attaches to instances or enforce licence counts for BYOL products.

questions.question: A workload in a single AZ is taken offline when that AZ has a utility-power incident. The architect spreads the workload across 3 AZs in the same Region. Why does this design eliminate the single-AZ failure?
options: AZs are labels for the same datacentre with no real physical isolation or single-failure boundary
AZs share power, cooling, and network feeds
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling, and network
Multi-AZ deployments always double the cost regardless of architecture
questions.explanation: Each AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power/network. They're connected with low-latency links but isolated from each other's failures. Multi-AZ = high availability. ELB + Auto Scaling + RDS Multi-AZ = HA architecture. The other options are incorrect: AZs are labels for the same datacentre with no real physical isolation or single-failure boundary — false; AZs are physically separate facilities with independent failure domains so a single AZ failure does not cascade. AZs share power, cooling, and network feeds — false; each AZ has independent power, cooling, and connectivity so that a single utility failure in one AZ does not affect the others. Multi-AZ deployments always double the cost regardless of architecture — false; cost depends on the specific service and configuration; deploying across AZs is the standard architecture for high availability without necessarily doubling overall cost.

questions.question: An enterprise wants AWS to set up a multi-account 'landing zone' for them — pre-baked OUs, guardrails enforced via SCPs, a 'log archive' account, an 'audit' account, an Account Factory for new accounts. They want this in a few clicks, not via custom CloudFormation. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Data Center Inventory
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements
AWS IAM role lifecycle manager
AWS Control Tower
questions.explanation: Control Tower builds a Landing Zone with: Log Archive account, Audit account, and an Account Factory. Guardrails (preventive = SCPs, detective = Config Rules) enforce compliance automatically across all accounts. The other options are incorrect: AWS Data Center Inventory — not a real AWS service; no AWS product provides pre-baked multi-account landing zone setup with automated OUs and audit accounts. AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements; it does not set up multi-account landing zones with SCP guardrails, log-archive accounts, or account factory provisioning. AWS IAM role lifecycle manager — not a real AWS service; no AWS product uses that name for managing multi-account landing zones or pre-baked audit account structures.

questions.question: Finance asks BI for monthly KPI dashboards over Athena/Redshift/RDS data, accessible in a browser, no servers to operate, with per-reader pricing. Which AWS service fits?
options: Amazon CloudWatch — operational-metrics dashboards over AWS infrastructure metrics
Amazon QuickSight — serverless BI service with dashboards over S3 / Redshift
AWS Glue — managed ETL service for cataloguing and transforming data
AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs of AWS API calls
questions.explanation: QuickSight connects to dozens of data sources and enables self-service BI with SPICE (in-memory computation engine). ML Insights adds anomaly detection and forecasting. Pay-per-session pricing model. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudWatch — operational-metrics dashboards over AWS infrastructure metrics; not a BI tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing. AWS Glue — managed ETL service for cataloguing and transforming data; does not render BI dashboards over Athena, Redshift, or RDS for finance users. AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs of AWS API calls; not a BI dashboard tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing.

questions.question: A finance team compares EC2 cost models: (a) ~12 months of free usage on small instance types, (b) per-hour pay-as-you-go, (c) 1- or 3-year commitment with 40-72% discount, (d) interruptible spare capacity at up to 90% off. Which mapping is correct?
options: All four EC2 cost models have the same effective hourly rate
Spot is dedicated long-running reserved capacity contracted for the full usage period
Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand at every comparable instance size
Free Tier = 12-mo free; On-Demand = pay-as-you-go; Reserved = 1/3-yr commit discount; Spot = interruptible spare capacity
questions.explanation: EC2 pricing: On-Demand (full price, flexible), RI Standard (fixed type, ~72% off, 1-3yr), RI Convertible (~66% off, can change type), Spot (bid on spare capacity, cheapest, interruptible with 2-min notice), Savings Plans (flexible commitment). The other options are incorrect: All four EC2 cost models have the same effective hourly rate — false; Free Tier provides free usage, On-Demand bills on-demand, Reserved gives discounts, and Spot uses interruptible spare capacity at steep reductions. Spot is dedicated long-running reserved capacity contracted for the full usage period — false; Spot provides interruptible spare-capacity instances priced hourly, not committed months-long terms. Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand at every comparable instance size — false; Reserved Instances provide a significant discount over On-Demand in exchange for a 1- or 3-year usage commitment.
